hook: Marigolds are there to be smelled, not seen.
fact: On Dia de los Muertos the cempasuchil marigold is spread in paths and on altars because its scent, not its color, is believed to lead the dead home. The flower is native to Mexico and was used in the ritual long before the Spanish arrived.
backbone: The flowers are a set of directions.
sources: Mexican ethnographic accounts of Dia de Muertos practice; cempasuchil as Tagetes erecta, native to Mexico

hook: It is 2 days, and the children come first.
fact: November 1 is Dia de los Angelitos, held for children who died. November 2 is for the adults. The altar is built for different people on different days, and the food on it changes to match who is expected.
backbone: The 2 dates are not a long weekend. They are 2 different guest lists.
sources: Catholic All Saints and All Souls calendar merged with Mexican practice; widely documented in regional custom

hook: The harvest moon is named after overtime.
fact: Most of the year the moon comes up about 45 minutes later each night. Around the autumn equinox it is 25 to 30 minutes for several nights running, so there is no dark gap after sunset. That is the light they were named after, and they used it to keep working.
backbone: It is not brighter. It is just punctual.
sources: the shallow angle of the ecliptic to the horizon at the autumnal equinox; standard astronomical explanation
bed_desc: warm modern instrumental, open and slow

hook: Harvest used to mean the season, not the work.
fact: The Old English haerfest meant autumn itself. It only came to mean the act of gathering crops later, and autumn had to borrow a new name. Autumn arrived from Latin by way of French in the 1300s.
backbone: We renamed the season after the chore we did in it.
sources: Oxford English Dictionary entries for harvest and autumn; Old English haerfest

hook: A good cranberry bounces.
fact: A ripe cranberry has air pockets inside, so it bounces and a bruised one does not. John Webb worked it out in the 1880s by pouring his crop down the barn stairs because his wooden leg would not carry it. Growers still sort on the bounce.
backbone: The sorting method is the berry failing a jump test.
sources: the bounce board attributed to New Jersey grower John Webb; still the basis of modern separators

hook: There was no pie at the 1621 meal.
fact: Edward Winslow wrote the only eyewitness account of it. There was deer and wildfowl. There was no butter and no wheat flour for a crust, and potatoes had not reached New England yet. Pie came later, and so did almost everything else on the table now.
backbone: The meal we copy every year is mostly a 19th century invention.
sources: Edward Winslow's letter in Mourt's Relation, 1622

hook: It ran 3 days and most of the guests were Wampanoag.
fact: Winslow records roughly 90 Wampanoag men present against about 50 colonists, and the gathering lasting 3 days. The colonists were outnumbered close to 2 to 1 at their own harvest meal.
backbone: It was not a dinner. It was a 3 day diplomatic event.
sources: Edward Winslow, letter of December 11, 1621, in Mourt's Relation, London 1622: "their greatest king Massasoyt, with some ninetie men whom for three dayes we entertained and feasted"

hook: A magazine editor asked for 36 years and got a yes in 5 days.
fact: Sarah Josepha Hale started calling for a national day of thanksgiving in 1827 and began writing to presidents in 1846. Taylor, Fillmore, Pierce and Buchanan all declined. She wrote to Lincoln on September 28, 1863. He proclaimed it on October 3. She also wrote Mary Had a Little Lamb.
backbone: The holiday exists because 1 woman would not drop it.
sources: Hale in Ladies Magazine from 1827 and Godey's Lady's Book from 1846; her letter to Lincoln dated September 28, 1863; the proclamation of October 3, 1863

hook: A president moved Thanksgiving and the country split over it.
fact: Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving a week earlier in 1939 to lengthen the Christmas shopping season. That year 23 states kept the old date, 22 took the new one, and Colorado, Mississippi and Texas held both. Congress fixed it to the 4th Thursday in 1941.
backbone: For 2 years there were 2 Thanksgivings, depending on the state line.
sources: FDR's 1939 proclamation; the joint resolution of December 1941 setting the fourth Thursday

hook: The first Macy's Thanksgiving parade was not called that.
fact: The 1924 parade ran 6 miles with bears, elephants, camels and monkeys on loan from the Central Park Zoo. It was called the Macy's Christmas Parade. Balloons replaced the animals in 1927, which is also the year the name changed.
backbone: The balloons were a safety fix.
sources: Macy's parade history, 1924 first procession and 1927 introduction of balloons

hook: They used to let the balloons go on purpose.
fact: From 1928 the balloons were let go at the end of the parade on purpose, built to leak slowly, with a return address and 100 dollars for whoever sent one back. It stopped after 1932, when another pilot nearly crashed trying to catch one in the air.
backbone: The end of the parade was a scavenger hunt over New York.
sources: Macy's parade accounts of the balloon release years and the 1932 aircraft incident
bed_desc: scratchy period recording, late 1920s dance band

hook: The bird is American and the name is not.
fact: The bird is American. Turkish traders sold a different African bird into England first and the name stuck to the wrong one. Turkey calls it hindi, for India. France got dinde from poulet d'Inde. Portuguese sailors gave it peru. Everybody named it after somewhere it is not from.
backbone: It was named after the wrong continent and it stuck.
sources: Oxford English Dictionary on turkey; the Levant trade route attribution

hook: Wild turkeys sleep in trees.
fact: A wild turkey flies up into a tree at dusk and spends the night there, off the ground and out of reach. It can hit roughly 55 miles an hour in a short burst. The bird we eat is the same animal, bred heavy enough that it never gets up there.
backbone: What we bred out of it was the way up.
sources: state wildlife agency accounts of wild turkey roosting and burst flight speed; breed weight is why the domestic bird is flightless in practice
plate_desc: silhouettes high in a bare oak, last light
bed_desc: warm modern instrumental, open and slow

hook: Pulling the wishbone is about 2500 years old.
fact: The Etruscans treated the fowl's furcula as an oracle and the Romans picked the habit up from them. The bone was stroked for a wish before anyone thought to break it, and the breaking came later when there were not enough bones to go round.
backbone: A table game outlived the civilisation that started it.
sources: the Etruscan link and alectryomancy are well attested for the 8th to 3rd century BCE. The detail about drying the bone and stroking it for wishes comes from popular retellings, not from primary scholarship, so the caption says the practice is roughly 2500 years old and stops there

hook: The turkey is not what makes you sleepy.
fact: Tryptophan sits at about the same level in all protein, and chicken, cheese and fish carry as much or more. It also loses the race into the brain against other amino acids. The carbohydrates clear its competition out of the way, so it is the stuffing and the potatoes doing it.
backbone: You are not drugged. You are full.
sources: nutritional comparisons of tryptophan content; the amino acid competition at the blood brain barrier
bed_desc: warm modern instrumental, open and slow

hook: Green bean casserole was written by a woman at a soup company in 1955.
fact: Dorcas Reilly ran the Campbell's test kitchen and wrote it in 1955 out of 6 ingredients that were already in the pantry. She called it Green Bean Bake.
backbone: It was designed to be makeable from what was already in the cupboard.
sources: Campbell's Soup Company records; the Reilly recipe card at the National Inventors Hall of Fame

hook: Thanksgiving football is older than the national holiday is settled.
fact: Yale and Princeton played on Thanksgiving Day in 1876, 13 years after Lincoln's proclamation and 65 years before Congress fixed the date. The professional game joined the tradition in 1920.
backbone: The game got there before the calendar did.
sources: intercollegiate football records for the 1876 Yale Princeton Thanksgiving fixture

hook: The Thanksgiving special serves toast and popcorn.
fact: The 1973 special serves toast, popcorn fried in a pan, pretzel sticks, jelly beans and sundaes, on a ping pong table in the yard. Peppermint Patty, who invited herself, is furious about it.
backbone: The most quoted Thanksgiving meal on television is not a meal.
sources: A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving, CBS, November 1973
bed_desc: warm jazz piano trio, newly played, not the original score

hook: The turkey pardon started as a way to dodge a question.
fact: George H. W. Bush gave the first official pardon on November 17, 1989. Reagan had used the word first, in 1987, deflecting a question about pardoning 2 men over Iran-Contra.
backbone: An old favour became a ceremony the moment somebody named it.
sources: White House records of the 1989 presidential turkey presentation

hook: They never called themselves Pilgrims.
fact: They called themselves Saints. Other colonists called them Old Comers or the Forefathers. The name we use caught on after Daniel Webster said "Pilgrim Fathers" at the 1820 bicentennial, about 200 years after they landed.
backbone: The name was applied long after the people were gone.
sources: William Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation; the popularisation of Pilgrims in 19th century oratory

hook: Corn, beans and squash were planted as 1 system.
fact: Corn gives the beans something to climb. The beans pull nitrogen out of the air into the soil and hold the corn steady in wind. The squash leaves shade the ground, keep the water in and crowd the weeds out. 3 crops, 1 mound, almost no tending.
backbone: 3 crops doing 1 another's maintenance.
sources: documented Haudenosaunee and wider Indigenous companion planting; nitrogen fixation in legumes
bed_desc: warm modern instrumental, open and slow

hook: Leaves do not fall. They get pushed.
fact: The tree builds the breaking point in spring, at the base of each leaf stalk, while it is still growing. In autumn it cuts the water off, then a layer of cells swells until the weak-walled cells above them snap. The leaf is let go on a schedule set months earlier.
backbone: Nothing about autumn is an accident.
sources: plant physiology on the abscission layer, auxin withdrawal and cell elongation
plate_desc: 1 leaf stalk where it meets the branch, close
bed_desc: warm modern instrumental, open and slow

hook: The language spoken at that harvest had no speakers left. It has them again.
fact: Nobody is recorded speaking Wôpanâak after about 1833. In 1993 Jessie Little Doe Baird began rebuilding it from what had been written down: a 1663 Bible translation, and deeds and wills written by speakers themselves. It is being taught in Wampanoag households now.
backbone: The people at that table are not a historical detail. They are a nation with a language.
sources: Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project; the 1663 Eliot Bible, the first complete Bible printed in this hemisphere; Baird MacArthur Fellowship 2010
bed_desc: 1 plucked string, sparse. No recording of the language exists from 1663, which is the fact

hook: Gratitude journaling works better once a week than 3 times a week.
fact: In a 2005 study, people who wrote down what they were grateful for once a week measurably improved. The group doing it 3 times a week got no benefit, and some came out slightly worse. Doing it more often turned noticing into a chore.
backbone: This one fails by being overdone, not by being skipped.
sources: Lyubomirsky, Sheldon and Schkade 2005, once a week against 3 times a week. Effect sizes in this literature are modest and not every measure moves, so the caption claims the frequency finding and nothing more
bed_desc: warm modern instrumental, open and slow

hook: The most quoted Thanksgiving document was not written by the man who signed it.
fact: Lincoln set the last Thursday in November on October 3, 1863, months after Gettysburg. He did not write it. The proclamation is in Secretary of State William Seward's handwriting.
backbone: It was declared at the worst possible moment and never missed a year.
sources: Lincoln's proclamation of October 3, 1863

hook: No gifts. No costumes. Just the table.
fact: Every other holiday on the calendar wants you to buy something or wear something. This 1 asks you to turn up and eat with people.
backbone: That is the whole assignment.
sources: none. This is a closing thought and not a factual claim
verified: n/a, this is a framing and not a claim
